articles.title: Affiliate Marketing in 2026
articles.excerpt: Affiliate marketing keeps evolving as digital products, user behavior, and tracking technologies change. Here's what is shaping partner programs in 2026 and how teams adapt to stay competitive.
articles.introHtml:
Affiliate marketing continues to evolve as digital products, user behavior, and tracking technologies change. What worked a few years ago no longer guarantees results today. In this article, we explore the main trends shaping affiliate marketing in 2026 and how publishers, advertisers, and partners can adapt to stay competitive.

The goal is no longer just traffic volume. Instead, quality, trust, and long-term relationships are becoming the foundation of successful affiliate strategies.

sections.title: Why Traditional Affiliate Models Are Losing Effectiveness
sections.bodyHtml:
For many years, affiliate marketing relied heavily on banner ads, coupon websites, and last-click attribution. While these methods still exist, their impact is gradually declining.

Users are more selective about what they click, and ad blindness is a real challenge. In addition, privacy regulations and browser restrictions make tracking more complex than ever.

subsections.title: Some of the key reasons traditional models struggle today include:
subsections.bodyHtml:
• Increased competition across almost every niche
  • Lower trust in generic promotional content
  • Limited visibility into the full customer journey
  • Changes in tracking technologies and cookies

sections.title: Content-Driven Affiliate Strategies
sections.bodyHtml:
High-quality content has become the most powerful tool in affiliate marketing. Instead of focusing on aggressive promotion, modern affiliates invest in educational, helpful, and experience-based content such as in-depth blog articles, honest product comparisons, tutorials, walkthroughs, and case studies based on real usage. Rather than listing dozens of products with referral links, successful affiliates usually focus on a smaller selection and clearly explain why each option fits a specific audience.

A good example of a content-first approach can be seen on platforms like affiliate.makeberry.com where clarity, structure, and user experience play a major role.

articles.title: SiGMA Central Europe B2C Awards 2025

articles.title: Prague Gaming & TECH Summit
articles.excerpt: Three days of conversations on retention, compliance, and creative throughput. Our biggest takeaways from the Prague Gaming & TECH Summit floor and what they mean for partner programs.
articles.introHtml:
The Prague Gaming & TECH Summit is one of the densest events on the Central European calendar — three days of operator, supplier, and affiliate conversations under one roof. We sent a small team focused on retention, compliance, and creative throughput, and came back with a clear list of priorities.

This recap is for partners and advertisers who could not be on-site but want a short, opinionated summary of what mattered.

sections.title: What Stood Out on the Floor
sections.bodyHtml:
The most repeated topics across stages and side rooms were retention economics, the operational cost of compliance, and the speed at which creative is now produced and tested. The market is clearly moving from raw acquisition spend to a more disciplined, lifecycle-driven view of player value.

Smaller, focused teams that ship fast were consistently outperforming larger, slower setups — a pattern we hear from our own partners every quarter.

subsections.title: The most actionable talking points we noted:
subsections.bodyHtml:
• Retention curves now matter more than first-deposit volume
  • Compliance is becoming a creative constraint, not just a legal one
  • Creative testing cycles are dropping from weeks to days
  • Data partnerships are replacing one-way reporting

sections.title: What We Are Bringing Back to Partners
sections.bodyHtml:
Internally, the summit reinforced three priorities: faster creative iteration with our top affiliates, a tighter feedback loop on player quality data, and clearer compliance guidance baked directly into the partner UI.

You can already see early steps of this work on affiliate.makeberry.com — and we'll have more to share with active partners in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Affiliate Marketing in 2026: A Deeper Cut
articles.excerpt: A second look at affiliate marketing in 2026 — this time focused on the operational mechanics: attribution, partner segmentation, and where the smart money is going.
articles.introHtml:
The first edition of this series looked at why traditional affiliate models are losing momentum. This second edition zooms in on the operational details: how leading networks segment partners, how attribution is changing under privacy pressure, and where budget is actually moving in 2026.

The headline is simple — quality, trust, and long-term relationships are reshaping how partner marketing performs.

sections.title: Partner Segmentation Beyond Volume
sections.bodyHtml:
Volume-only ranking is no longer enough. Networks that perform well in 2026 segment partners by retention quality, support load, content style, and product fit. The result: smaller cohorts of partners get tailored terms and faster decision-making, instead of one flat program for everyone.

This shift requires cleaner data and tighter collaboration between BD, finance, and product — but it pays off in churn, payout efficiency, and partner NPS.

subsections.title: Signals that we now weigh as heavily as raw volume:
subsections.bodyHtml:
• 30/60/90-day retention of referred users
  • Average revenue per referred user vs. cohort baseline
  • Time-to-first-conversion across creative formats
  • Compliance score and creative review velocity

sections.title: Where Affiliate Budget Is Actually Going
sections.bodyHtml:
Budget is consolidating around fewer, higher-trust partners, while exploration budget is reserved for fast tests with smaller, content-led teams. Coupon and incentive traffic still has a place, but only where it complements a clear retention story — not as a stand-alone bet.

Two themes kept coming back across those conversations: long-term partner programs are quietly outperforming short-term campaigns, and teams with strong internal culture are easier to spot from the outside than people think.

articles.title: Prague Gaming Summit: Side Conversations That Mattered
articles.excerpt: The deals and ideas from the Prague Gaming & TECH Summit rarely happen on the main stage. A recap of the side conversations that actually shaped our partner roadmap.
articles.introHtml:
The Prague Gaming & TECH Summit is a public event with a private layer underneath it. Most of the value for our team came from corridor conversations, dinner tables, and quiet rooms away from the main stage. This recap focuses on those.

Some takeaways are tactical, some are cultural — together they already changed how we plan the next two quarters.

sections.title: What Partners Were Quietly Saying
sections.bodyHtml:
Off-stage, almost every serious conversation revolved around three pressures: retention quality vs. acquisition cost, the operational cost of new compliance requirements, and the speed at which creative needs to be reproduced and localized.

Partners who already invested in their internal data, creative, and compliance stack are pulling ahead. Partners who treated those as cost centers are starting to feel the gap.

subsections.title: Recurring topics in side conversations:
subsections.bodyHtml:
• Migration from generic creatives to brand-led ones
  • Heavier focus on multi-market localization
  • Tighter integration between affiliate and CRM teams
  • Demand for clearer, partner-facing compliance guidance

sections.title: What We Are Doing About It
sections.bodyHtml:
We left Prague with a small, opinionated list: invest more in localized creative kits, expose more of our compliance guidance directly inside the partner UI, and accelerate the rollout of our extended reporting layer.

You can track most of these changes through affiliate.makeberry.com, and active partners will see them land first inside the dashboard.

articles.title: Affiliate Marketing in 2026: Adapt or Stand Still
articles.excerpt: How publishers, advertisers, and partners can adapt to stay competitive in 2026 — practical adjustments rather than abstract trends.
articles.introHtml:
This third edition is intentionally practical. Less theory, more concrete steps that publishers, advertisers, and partners can apply this quarter to stay competitive in 2026 — without rebuilding their entire stack.

The underlying principle is unchanged: programs that win are the ones that protect quality and trust, even when growth becomes uncomfortable.

sections.title: What Publishers Should Adjust First
sections.bodyHtml:
For publishers, the highest-leverage move in 2026 is consolidation. Fewer offers, deeper coverage, more first-hand experience per recommendation. The goal is not to reduce inventory for its own sake — it is to free up the creative and editorial bandwidth needed to compete on trust.

The most effective publishers we work with treat their offer list like a product catalog: opinionated, curated, and refreshed on a real schedule.

subsections.title: Concrete adjustments to consider this quarter:
subsections.bodyHtml:
• Trim under-performing offers from the front page
  • Refresh the top 10 reviews with first-hand observations
  • Add structured comparison tables where they are missing
  • Audit outbound links and tracking for accuracy

sections.title: What Advertisers Should Demand From Their Network
sections.bodyHtml:
From the advertiser side, the bar is rising. Better cohort reporting, faster creative approvals, and clearer partner curation are no longer nice-to-haves — they are the baseline expected from a serious network in 2026.

If you want to see how we approach those expectations on our side, head to affiliate.makeberry.com and request a partner walkthrough.

articles.title: From the Archive: Affiliate Marketing in 2026
articles.excerpt: An archived look at how affiliate strategies evolved in early 2026 — what teams expected, what actually happened, and which calls aged the best.
articles.introHtml:
An archived look at how affiliate strategies evolved in early 2026. Half retrospective, half checklist: what teams expected at the start of the year, what actually happened, and which strategic calls aged the best.

Useful as a sanity-check before locking in the next planning cycle.

sections.title: Predictions vs. Reality
sections.bodyHtml:
Most early-2026 predictions held up at a directional level — content-led affiliates would outperform coupon-only ones, attribution would get harder, and trust would beat volume. The interesting part is in the second decimal: how those shifts actually played out month by month.

A few calls aged better than expected, others needed quiet revision once real data came in.

subsections.title: Predictions that aged especially well:
subsections.bodyHtml:
• Tighter integration of affiliate and CRM teams
  • Rise of content-driven affiliate strategies
  • Slow decline of last-click-only attribution models
  • Higher demand for transparent partner reporting

sections.title: What Quietly Changed in the Background
sections.bodyHtml:
The less-discussed change in 2026 was operational: how networks talk about quality, how partners share data, and how advertisers measure trust. It happened without big announcements, but it reshaped how budgets are allocated quarter by quarter.

If you want to see how we describe quality in plain language to our own partners, that part of the story lives on affiliate.makeberry.com.

That internal effect is harder to measure, but it shows up in retention, in willingness to take on hard problems, and in how the team talks about the company in private.

Awards come and go. What we want to be remembered for is more boring and more durable: predictable partner programs, healthy player quality for advertisers, and a team that is genuinely good to work with.

articles.title: From the Archive: Prague Gaming & TECH Summit
articles.excerpt: Notes from the Prague Gaming & TECH Summit floor, archived for the next planning cycle — the patterns that survived, and the ones that did not.
articles.introHtml:
Notes from the Prague Gaming & TECH Summit floor, archived for the next planning cycle. Some patterns survived the year, others quietly disappeared. This is a short, opinionated post-mortem.

Mostly useful for teams preparing their own event strategy or roadmap reviews.

sections.title: Patterns That Survived the Year
sections.bodyHtml:
The patterns that survived the year were the unglamorous ones: investing in player quality data, designing programs around long-term partner relationships, and treating compliance as part of the product rather than a checkbox at the end.

None of these were headline-worthy in Prague — but they were the ones quietly rewarded by the market over the following months.

subsections.title: Patterns we will keep investing in:
subsections.bodyHtml:
• Long-term partner programs over short campaigns
  • Compliance as a product surface, not just a back-office task
  • Tighter feedback loops between affiliates and product teams
  • Honest reporting, even when numbers are uncomfortable

sections.title: Patterns That Did Not Make It
sections.bodyHtml:
Some of the loudest themes in Prague faded by the end of the year — purely volume-led narratives, generic creative bundles, and the assumption that compliance could be solved with tooling alone. They sounded compelling on stage and underperformed in the wild.

To see what we actually doubled down on instead, the most up-to-date overview lives on affiliate.makeberry.com.
